items.title: The hardest known natural substance and a pencil lead are the same element
items.claim: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs hardness scale. Graphite scores 1-2 (it leaves a streak on paper). Both are 100 percent pure carbon. Same element, same atoms, vastly different materials.

options.text: Diamond is sp3 hybridised with every carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others (a rigid 3D network); graphite is sp2 with strong in-plane bonds but only weak van der Waals forces between layers
Diamond and graphite have different isotopes of carbon

items.reveal:
In diamond every carbon shares electrons with four neighbours arranged at 109.5 degrees. The result is a giant covalent lattice that cannot be deformed without breaking strong sigma bonds in many directions at once.

In graphite each carbon bonds strongly to three neighbours in a flat hexagonal sheet. Sheets stack but are held together only by weak dispersion forces. Layers slide past each other easily — hence the pencil-streak behaviour.

Thermodynamically, graphite is actually the more stable form at room temperature and pressure by 2.9 kJ/mol. Diamond is metastable — it would convert to graphite, given long enough.
items.why: Identity of an element is not enough to determine properties. Bonding arrangement (allotropy) can transform a substance utterly.

items.title: The hardest natural material and pencil 'lead' are the same element
items.claim: Diamond scores 10 on the Mohs scale, the maximum. Graphite scores 1-2 — it streaks on paper. Both are 100 percent pure carbon. Identical atoms, opposite mechanical properties.

options.text: Diamond contains stronger isotopes of carbon
Diamond's sp3 carbons form a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice (all sigma bonds); graphite's sp2 carbons form strong hexagonal sheets held together only by weak dispersion forces, so sheets slide
Diamond is at higher temperature when it forms

items.reveal:
Diamond: every carbon bonded tetrahedrally to four others, all strong sigma bonds. No mobile electrons (insulator), no slip planes (hard).

Graphite: each carbon sp2-hybridised, three in-plane sigma bonds plus a delocalised pi system across the sheet. Sheets stack 0.335 nm apart, held only by van der Waals forces. The pi electrons conduct along the layers; the layers slide past each other — hence the pencil streak.

Thermodynamically, graphite is more stable than diamond by 2.9 kJ/mol at room temperature and pressure. Diamond is metastable; only a kinetic barrier stops it converting to graphite over geological time.
items.why: Element identity isn't enough — bonding arrangement (allotropy) can transform a substance utterly.

items.title: Water dissolves more things than any other liquid
items.claim: Water is called 'the universal solvent'. It dissolves more substances than any other liquid — salts, sugars, gases, many organic molecules. Yet it has only three atoms and a simple structure.
items.prompt: What makes water such a versatile solvent?

options.text: Water is highly polar (large dipole), forms hydrogen bonds with H-bond donors and acceptors, and has a high dielectric constant (around 80) that weakens ionic attractions enough for ions to separate and become solvated
Water is the only liquid on Earth that occurs naturally

items.reveal:
Water's bent shape and large O-H bond polarity give a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 debye. Each water molecule can form up to 4 hydrogen bonds — two as donor, two as acceptor.

Water's dielectric constant of about 80 (vs about 2 for hexane) means it screens ionic charges strongly: a cation and anion that would attract each other electrostatically in vacuum are 80 times less attracted in water, so they separate.

Non-polar substances (oils, wax) lack matching interactions and so won't dissolve. 'Universal' is overstating things — water is just a brilliant solvent for polar and ionic species, and we mostly care about polar and ionic species.
items.why: Water is treated as a passive background. Its chemistry actively shapes whether ions stay dissolved or precipitate.
